Iceland’s Transport and Logistics Sector Faces Credit Freeze, Isavia Ohf Impacted

REYKJAVIK, June 14—A credit freeze affecting Iceland’s transportation and logistics sector has triggered a mounting financial crisis, with several firms, including airport operator Isavia Ohf, reporting severe liquidity constraints and operational disruptions. The crisis, which began earlier this week, has rapidly intensified amid mounting concerns over short-term debt refinancing and the withdrawal of commercial lending lines.

Industry sources said the freeze originated after a sharp downgrade in sector credit ratings by domestic lenders, prompting banks to tighten lending criteria and halt renewals of revolving credit facilities. “The sudden halt in credit has left us unable to meet several key payments,” said Jónas Helgason, chief financial officer at Isavia Ohf. “We are working with our partners and authorities to stabilize the situation, but the uncertainty is unprecedented.”

Other companies, such as freight hauler Norðurgata Logistics, have reported difficulties maintaining payroll and fuel purchases. “We’re facing a daily struggle to keep our trucks on the road,” said Edda Kristinsdóttir, CEO of Norðurgata Logistics. “Several scheduled shipments have already been postponed.”

According to the Icelandic Transport Association, up to 60% of companies in the sector are now experiencing acute cash shortages. “The industry is facing the most severe financial stress since the 2008 banking crisis,” said the association’s chair, Magnús Sigurðsson. “We urgently need coordinated action from policymakers and lenders to avoid a wave of insolvencies.”

Union representatives have warned that job losses are likely if the situation persists. “Our members are deeply concerned about their livelihoods,” said Ólafur Sveinsson, a spokesperson for the Transport Workers’ Union. “We call on all stakeholders to find solutions to preserve employment.”

The government has not yet announced sector-specific measures. Analysts said the extent of the disruption will depend on how quickly credit flows can be restored. The crisis remains ongoing, and sector leaders are meeting with officials to seek emergency support.
